opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think the core judgment held up better than I expected, though for reasons that were only partly clear to me at the time.

When I started on XGBoost, deep learning was beginning to take off, and a lot of people assumed neural networks would simply eat everything. My bet was more practical than ideological. I kept seeing that real-world data, especially tabular data with mixed feature types, missing values, and messy distributions, wasn't the kind of data neural networks handled gracefully. Tree models were robust there. You didn't need careful normalization, they were fairly interpretable, and with gradient boosting you could get very strong accuracy without heroic tuning.

What I underestimated, and what I'd now say was the more important judgment, was that the systems side mattered as much as the algorithm. Gradient boosting already existed. What made the difference was making it scalable: handling sparsity properly, parallelizing tree construction, being careful about cache access and out-of-core computation, and running in distributed settings. That experience shaped how I think about machine learning: the algorithm and the system have to be designed together, and that's carried into my later work on things like TVM and ML compilation.

Where I'd be more humble is that I didn't fully anticipate how long tree models would stay relevant. Even now, for many tabular problems, a well-tuned boosted tree is still a very strong baseline, sometimes the best answer. But I also wouldn't frame it as trees versus neural networks anymore. The more lasting lesson is to pick the tool that fits the structure of the data and the constraints people actually face, and then do the engineering work to make it usable at scale. A lot of XGBoost's impact came from people simply being able to download it, run it on their own problems, and have it work. That accessibility was, in hindsight, as much a part of the bet as the modeling choice itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think the honest answer is that the judgment was less about a grand vision and more about a series of practical bets that happened to compound well.

When I started working on what became XGBoost, around 2014, the deep learning wave was already building. A lot of people, including some of my peers, thought trees were a bit old-fashioned. Gradient boosting was known, it worked, but it wasn't where the excitement was. So the first judgment was simply: this is a method that reliably works on tabular, structured data, and nobody has built it really well as a system. That gap seemed worth filling.

The second judgment was to treat it as a systems problem rather than purely an algorithmic one. I came at it from a background where I cared about how things actually ran on hardware, cache behavior, sparsity, parallelism. The regularized objective and the second-order approximation were important, but what made people adopt it was that it was fast and handled real data with missing values gracefully. I underestimated at the time how much that mattered. Kaggle competitions turned out to be the proving ground, and once practitioners saw it win repeatedly, the adoption took care of itself.

If I'm critical of myself, I'd say I didn't fully anticipate how long trees would remain dominant on tabular data. I thought of XGBoost as a solid tool I was building before moving on to other things. It's now more than a decade later and deep models still don't consistently beat well-tuned boosted trees on that kind of data. So the bet was more correct than I knew, partly for reasons I didn't fully understand at the time, like the inductive bias trees have for heterogeneous features.

The other lesson I took, which shaped my later work on TVM and MLC, is that a good algorithm with a great implementation and an open community beats a slightly better algorithm that lives in a paper. That judgment I'd make again without hesitation.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think the judgment was useful, but I wouldn’t describe it as knowing that tree models were going to be the right answer. It was more about recognizing that they were a strong starting point and that there was room to make gradient boosting more practical.

Trees have a useful inductive bias: they can capture nonlinear relationships and interactions without requiring you to specify those relationships in advance. But the quality of the model is only part of the story. Training efficiency, memory use, and how easily people can experiment also matter. Improving those things lets people try more ideas and ultimately build better models.

So I would separate two judgments. One was that boosted trees were worth investing in; I still think that was sound. The other would be that they should be the answer to every problem, and that’s not a conclusion I would draw. The broader lesson for me is to look at the learning method and the system together.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think the key judgment was that the choice of model and the design of the system had to go together. Trees were already a strong fit for many practical problems, especially tabular data. The opportunity was to make gradient boosting more efficient and scalable so that people could use it more easily.

I wouldn’t describe that as knowing in advance that trees would be the right answer everywhere. It was a practical direction: take an approach that worked well, understand its bottlenecks, and improve it. I still think that was a useful judgment, while recognizing that the best model depends on the problem.
